newsitem.title: CYPRUS: FEATURE - Cypriots get together to get along.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cypriots get together to get along.

text.p: They have been called traitors and wishy-washy liberals.
They have been publicly ridiculed.
Not surprisingly, Cypriots involved in bi-communal activities promoting the resolution of conflict on the divided island have kept a very low profile.
Some, like Greek Cypriot Katy Economidou, have started to take the criticism in their stride, developing a thick skin in the process.
"Well, they don't only call you traitors. I've heard worse. You get lots of curses as well," she said.

Economidou, 37, is one of about 3,000 Cypriots actively engaged in building bridges across the psychological barriers created by years of forced separation of the Greeks and Turks on the eastern Mediterranean island.

She is a leader of one of the bi-communal citizens' groups that have been meeting regularly for the past two years either in the U.N.-controlled buffer zone separating the communities or on the respective sides after pre-arranged visits.
From darts matches to gatherings of accountants and economists, meetings of people from either side of the barbed wire slicing through Cyprus are becoming daily events.
Those taking part are encouraged by the recently renewed -- if still fruitless -- attempts at dialogue between Greek Cypriot leader Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.
"It is a sign of rapproachement," said Adil Nami, a 53-year-old former health education officer and chairman of the 350-member Cyprus Turkish Peace Association.
Nami introduces himself as a "Cypriot Turk."
"It is better, no?" he asks of putting the emphasis on "Cypriot".
"Of course there are people who are sceptical at the prospects on Cyprus -- this situation has been with us for such a long time."
Building trust on the ruins of the past is not easy. There are decades of mistrust and animosity to overcome and painful memories to put aside.
Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been living separately since 1974, after a Turkish invasion sparked by a brief Greek Cypriot coup in the capital Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
But animosity dates from 1963 when a government created under the 1960 constitution and comprised of Greeks and Turks fell apart amid violence, prompting the dispatch of a U.N. peacekeeping force.
Underscoring the disparity of views, Greek Cypriots say the Cyprus problem started in 1974,which is when Turkish Cypriots say it ended.
"I remember my first meeting with a Turkish Cypriot and he started talking about the operation in 1974," said one Greek Cypriot.
"I didn't know what he was talking about. I thought he had surgery. Then I realised he was talking about the Turkish invasion. He called it a peace operation. I was dumbfounded."
OPPOSITION FROM WITHIN
Independent Greek Cypriot MP Marios Matsakis, dismisses the process of reconciliation as artificial.
"If the objective was to raise the level of confidence and promote goodwill between the communities there would be much easier ways of doing it," he said.

"Denktash could lift the restrictions on the freedom of movement on the 400 enclaved Greek Cypriots for a start," he said, referring to an ageing population of Greek Cypriots who have remained in the Turkish-held areas.
Matsakis has organised weekly protests at the U.N.-controlled checkpoint since last October to discourage tourists from visiting the north.
Cypriots who are engaged in bi-communal activities, he said, are misguided and brainwashed by the foreign diplomatic missions that sponsor their activities.
"Sitting around a table and then finding someone to talk to, to open up your feelings to, is the sort of thing bored rich housewives abroad would do," he said.
But one diplomat called those involved in the bicommunal activities "courageous and committed."
"I think it is made even more difficult for them because neither side has taken a clear stand on these gatherings," the diplomat said.
ENTRENCHED DIVISIONS
Social, business, even telephone links were severed in 1974, when 180,000 Greek Cypriot refugees were forced to move south as Turkish forces advanced.
A year later the division became more entrenched when 40,000 Turkish Cypriots living in the south left their homes to settle in the north.
"This problem is an open festering wound," said Constantinos Lordos, a Greek Cypriot businessman actively involved in bi-communal activities.

"It causes instability, as the recent past has shown us it can explode at any moment. It leaves us prey to scoundrels posing as patriots...We can't plan for tomorrow and the years to come and nor can our children."
Economidou and others like her acknowledge they cannot solve the Cyprus conflict, and do not attempt to. That is the job of politicians.

"This process has given citizens the chance to communicate and express their fears, hopes and aspirations. The wounds of the past are there and we are not ignoring them. This helps us understand why it is all happening."
It will be a long and torturous process.
Nami described the talks involving Clerides and Denktash as a "glimmer of hope" and urged continued pressure on political leaders to solve the problem.

"What keeps me there is a dream," Economidou said quietly. "We have a dream and this dream is for a better Cyprus, a better world and we derive strength from this dream because it is inspiring, enduring and deep."
